en: Under the semiotic apparatus already established, the sign is not a subjective ornament accompanying experience, since it operates as a public structure that organizes conduct and produces verifiable social effects, regardless of its physical truth or of individual mental states. Read this way, interpretation can be understood as an objective fact, since interpretants, that is, the relations of interpretation, do not necessarily depend on individual mental representations and are collectively verifiable <1>Eco</1><2>(Eco, 1991, p. 112)</2>.<3>p. 459</3>

Meaning is not reduced to a mental image, but operates as a relation instituted by the code, and even connotation becomes predictable through a shared lexicon, which makes it possible to describe symbolic losses by public criteria.<1>p. 459</1>

Two sources show that this position is social, not private. Ronaldo Helal, writing in the sociology of sport, observes that sport is one of the most solid social institutions of the modern world. That lens helps read continuous competitive ecosystems, in which seasons, rankings, rewards and shared memory turn a succession of matches into a place within a socially structured space. Ferraz Jr. treats reputation as a topos, that is, a commonplace of argument that the parties mobilize in legal debate, and the point also holds for the internal positions of user, participant, creator, moderated or sanctioned, whose persistent downgrading may reach the core of utility even without any interruption of access.

Helal observes that sport constitutes one of the most solid social institutions of the modern world and that its presence deeply penetrates everyday life, influencing habits, customs and modes of social insertion <1>Helal</1><2>(Helal, 1990, p. 11-12; p. 14)</2>.<3>p. 460</3>

When competition stabilizes through seasons, rankings, rewards, public circuits, shared memory and recognizable signs of prestige, enjoyment ceases to consist of a mere succession of matches and comes to operate as insertion into a socially structured space, in which belonging, reputation and biographical continuity are produced collectively.<1>p. 460-461</1>

In the sense indicated by Tércio Sampaio Ferraz Jr., elements such as reputation and stereotypes function as material topoi that can be mobilized in legal discussion, allowing the parties to present themselves as decent people, in good faith, aware of duties and rights and bearers of recognized public merit, as opposed to a minority or to interests described as deviant <1>Jr.</1><2>(Ferraz Jr., 1997, p. 84)</2>.<3>p. 464</3>

On platforms, the internal positions of user, participant, creator, moderated or sanctioned are likewise organized by roles and recognitions that condition enjoyment as a social practice, so that persistent downgrades of status and participation may reach the core of utility even without total interruption of access.<1>p. 464</1>
Why can the trajectory be worth more than the item?

Biographical continuity is the good that comes into view once time is taken into account. The consumer's trajectory is neither a passive record kept by the platform nor an informational deposit without a subject. It is a biographical result produced by repeated choices, performance, investment of time, acquisition, cooperation and accumulated signs of belonging and permanence, and it remains attributable to the consumer even when built under the law of the platform. That is why certain IOCs operate as trajectory assets, and not only as one-off utilities. What accumulates in them is memory, identity and recognition, and their unilateral suppression or reclassification cannot be treated as a mere technical variation.

Certain objects and marks of trajectory are worth less for what they “do” in utilitarian terms and more for what they mean in the ecosystem: status, rarity, belonging, memory of participation, distinction and social recognition.<1>p. 537</1>

The consumer's trajectory is not a mere passive “record” kept by the platform, nor an informational deposit without a subject. It is a biographical result produced by repeated choices, performance, investment of time, acquisition, cooperation, accumulation of signs of belonging and permanence in the ecosystem. Even though this construction takes place under the mediation of the Lex Plataformae, it remains attributable to the consumer as an expression of biographical continuity within the supply regime. For this reason, certain IOCs operate as trajectory assets and not merely as one-off utilities. What accumulates is a bundle of memory, identity and recognition, so that its unilateral suppression or reclassification cannot be treated as a simple irrelevant technical variation.<1>p. 537</1>

That is why the loss of a history, a title, a trajectory or a place of belonging can be more than the loss of an item, since what is consumed in these objects is also a symbolic position. Schreiber recalls that the protection of identity safeguards the faithful presentation of the person against compressions, falsifications and fixations produced by third parties. The lesson holds for the history of enjoyment and for the marks of participation, which enter into the way the consumer is recognized within the environment and, in certain cases, outside it. The loss of an account, a history or accumulated signs may, then, touch legally cognizable reputational and identity dimensions, but it does not always do so, because the passage from item to trajectory depends on the concrete object actually functioning as a biographical asset.
What is consumed, then, is not only functional performance, but also symbolic position.<1>p. 537</1>

The protection of identity does not protect only formal signs, but the faithful presentation of the person in their singularity, preventing compressions, falsifications and fixations produced by third parties <1>Schreiber</1><2>(Schreiber, 2014, p. 155-156; p. 216)</2>. On platforms, this means that the history of enjoyment, the signs of belonging and the accumulated marks of participation are not merely technical remnants of the experience; they take part in the way the consumer is recognized within the environment and, in certain cases, outside it. The IOC comes to operate as a biographical and identity asset.<3>p. 538</3>

In digital ecosystems, the loss of an account, of history, of accumulated signs and of continuity of trajectory may, therefore, transcend economic utility and touch legally cognizable reputational and identity dimensions.<1>p. 538</1>
Why does leaving the service not solve the loss?

Symbolic identity and personal integrity are linked by two dependence effects, symbolic captivity and identity captivity. The first is the platform's capacity to replace public repertoires of meaning with proprietary signs and internal grammars, which reduces external comparability. The second is a dependence in which the cost of exit is not exhausted by money or convenience, because leaving means losing narrative continuity and positions of recognition that exist, decisively, within the ecosystem. This is neither hypnosis of the consumer nor a psychologizing of the bond. It is a functional description of how architecture, curation and sanction can produce dependence.

The relevant loss appears when modulation ceases to be an ordinary variation of supply and comes to corrode, persistently, the possibility of acting with minimal predictability and of sustaining a position of use endowed with practical meaning. In this same register, symbolic identity and personal integrity are connected by two dependence effects that can be named symbolic captivity and identity captivity. The first designates the platform's capacity to replace public repertoires of meaning with proprietary signs and internal grammars that come to organize value, belonging and recognition, reducing external comparability and reordering the user's interpretable world under metrics, rarities, badges, rankings and administered visibility regimes. The second designates the form of dependence in which the cost of exit is not exhausted in financial or convenience dimensions, because it implies loss of narrative continuity and of positions of recognition whose existence takes place, decisively, within the ecosystem, through networks, histories, roles and internal circuits of value. In both cases, this is not hypnosis of the consumer nor a psychologization of the bond, but a functional description of how architecture, curation and sanction can produce dependence through exit costs and governance asymmetry, directly affecting agency and position of enjoyment.<1>p. 466</1>

For the lawyer, identity captivity explains why leaving the service is no simple answer for a dissatisfied consumer. Leaving breaks a narrative of the self built and validated within the environment, and it reaches the consumer's positional survival. The chapter on semiotic vulnerability describes how this dependence forms. For the protected goods, the consequence is that integrity and identity become governed variables of enjoyment, which calls for reinforced duties of qualified transparency, contestability, auditability and restoration.

Exit, therefore, does not present itself as a neutral consumption decision, since the cost is not limited to the price paid or to access to a utility, reaching the consumer's positional survival in a grammar of recognition that the ecosystem itself monopolizes.<1>p. 359</1>

Dependence consolidates because the platform concentrates the administration of metrics, of recognition criteria and of exposure trajectories, while it freely recalibrates what counts as adequate performance and which conduct will be rewardable or punishable. The result is an exit cost that is not exhausted in a one-off patrimonial loss, since it involves discontinuity of a narrative of the self that was built, measured and validated within the environment, in addition to loss of access to the very parameters that made this narrative intelligible.<1>p. 359</1>

This dependence on administered recognition is legally relevant because it makes integrity and identity governed variables of enjoyment and requires, on the dogmatic level, reinforced duties of qualified transparency, contestability, auditability and restoration proportional to the type of power exercised by the Lex Plataformae.<1>p. 359</1>
When does the loss cease to be an ordinary variation of the service?

Relevant losses can be organized in a matrix whose common axis is the impairment of the position of enjoyment over time, without depending on total interruption or on subjective assessment. The first loss is exclusion or significant limitation of participation, through blocks, restrictions or persistent downgrades. The second is substantial degradation of the conditions of use, when gradual reconfigurations, selective frictions, repeated instabilities or rule changes corrode the predictability of the experience. The third is the devaluation or erasure of signs of distinction and reputation, through alteration of metrics, badges, rarities, histories or visibility criteria. The fourth is the structural reconfiguration of access and recognition, when the consumer remains in the ecosystem but durably loses the capacity to occupy the position that made the object valuable.

The identification of relevant losses in the IOC can, then, be structured as a matrix that captures the harm without depending on total interruption or subjective assessment. The common axis is the impairment of the position of enjoyment over time, as a combination of practical conditions of use and agency in the environment and conditions of recognition, visibility and belonging that make up socially instituted utility.<1>p. 463</1>

Relevant losses, in this regime, include exclusion or significant limitation of participation when the platform prevents the normal exercise of the enjoyment bundle through blocks, restrictions or persistent downgrades. They include substantial degradation of the conditions of use when gradual reconfigurations, selective frictions, repeated instabilities or rule changes corrode the predictability and governability of the experience. They include the devaluation or erasure of signs of distinction and reputation when metrics, badges, rarities, histories or visibility criteria are altered so as to disfigure the stabilized symbolic utility. They include, finally, the structural reconfiguration of access and recognition when the consumer remains within the ecosystem but loses, durably, the capacity to occupy the position of enjoyment that made the object economically and socially valuable.<1>p. 463-464</1>

The part on the constitutional order adds a list of signs of relevant degradation, namely reputational exclusion, loss of functional equivalence, access restrictions, erasure of history and unilateral mutability of elements that structure the consumer's position. Any of these losses counts only when it meets three conditions. The downgrade must be significant and persistent, it must substantially alter the consumer's level of agency and position in the ecosystem, and the loss must be describable by verifiable criteria, under the filters of relevance and controllability.

The signs of relevant degradation also become clearer: reputational exclusion, loss of functional equivalence, access restrictions, erasure of history and unilateral mutability of elements that structure the consumer's position.<1>p. 543</1>

The delimitation is functional. In platform-governed enjoyment, part of the economically acquired value depends on architecturally produced conditions of participation, visibility, recognition and governability of the environment, and the relevant degradation of these conditions may objectively reach the enjoyment bundle without taking the form of total interruption. For this reason, the categories operate only when the downgrade is significant and persistent, when it substantially alters the level of agency and the consumer's position in the ecosystem, and when it can be described by verifiable criteria of loss in the IOC regime, under the filters of relevance and controllability.<1>p. 467-468</1>
What do end-of-season rewards show about symbolic identity?

An especially didactic example is the ranked rewards handed out at the end of each League of Legends season, in particular the Victorious skins and the borders tied to elo, which is the player's ranking tier. These signs do not operate as mere cosmetics, because they become social proof legible across the ecosystem, a historical and displayable reputation that the player carries on the account. The developer's support article requires the player to finish the season at Honor Level 3 or higher and to win 15 ranked matches, so the reward works as an institutional certification of merit, through which the platform defines what counts as winning and what counts as being recognized.

In League of Legends, a loading screen border associated with the user's ranking elo, or a progression icon, does not increase damage, does not change range, does not improve the win rate.<1>p. 268</1>

An especially didactic example of this symbolic identity as a public position appears in the end-of-season ranked rewards and, in particular, in the “Victorious” skins and the borders associated with elo. These signs do not operate as mere cosmetics, because they become social proof immediately legible in the ecosystem, stabilizing a form of reputation that is at once historical and displayable, since the player comes to carry, in the very symbolic body of the account, a mark of performance and temporal dedication recognized by third parties <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2026b)</2>.<3>p. 459-460</3>

The support article on end-of-season rewards is the space where the developer states as an objective requirement that the player “Finish the season with Honor Level 3 or higher” and also “Win 15 ranked matches” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2026b)</2>. In other words, the reward does not present itself as a neutral item, but as an institutional certification of ranking merit. Something publicly legible through which the platform defines not only what “winning” is, but also what “being recognized” is, so that merit converts into prestige capable of enjoyment through display.<3>p. 459-460</3>

The example shows how institutionalized symbolic identity can produce identity captivity. The sign of prestige depends on performance and also on maintaining a state of eligibility administered by disciplinary technologies of conduct, and the Honor Guide indicates that Honor levels 1 and 2 do not receive the ranked season rewards. Players come to manage their own behavior to preserve recognition and narrative continuity, because the relevant threat is no longer losing a match but missing a rare reward that consolidates status and that, once missed, cannot simply be bought again as an equivalent substitute.

Compliance ceases to be mere “following rules” and becomes a mechanism of self-preservation of a socially operative position in the ecosystem, in which the cost of leaving is not exhausted by time or money, but includes the loss of displayable historicity.<1>p. 462</1>

Obtaining the sign of prestige is conditioned not only on competitive performance, but also on maintaining a state of eligibility administered by disciplinary technologies of conduct, in which low Honor levels exclude the player from access to seasonal rewards <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2025a)</2>. In this dynamic, the subject comes to manage their own behavior with a focus on preserving recognition and narrative continuity, because the relevant threat is not only the loss of a match or of a functional convenience, but the frustration of a rare reward that consolidates status and that, once not received, cannot simply be repurchased as an equivalent substitute.<3>p. 461-462</3>

In the benefits table, the rule appears in operational form: under “Ranked Season Rewards”, Honor 1 and Honor 2 are listed as “No”, while Honor 3, 4 and 5 are listed as “Yes” (same page).<1>p. 461</1>

The legal point the case brings out is the regime of disciplined permanence that governs symbolic capital. The User Rules authorize bans, suspension, account termination, content removal, progress resets and chat and queue restrictions, whether or not a specific behavior is listed. In an end-of-season announcement, the company states that accounts involved in manipulating MMR, the hidden number the system uses to place each person in a balanced match, face suspension, removal of Honor level and exclusion from rewards. The risk of sanction thus falls on the integrity of agency and on symbolic identity, because the system makes prestige at once desirable and exposed to private governance.

The contract states that, to be eligible, the user must comply with “the acceptable use and conduct policies” published by the company and that, in case of violation, Riot may impose “temporary bans, suspension, or termination and deletion of the account”, as well as “content removal, resets of the user's progress”, “limitations on chat functionality” and “matchmaking queue restrictions and bans”, “regardless of whether a specific behavior is listed or not” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>.<3>p. 462</3>

In the text Fim da Temporada 2024 - Etapa 3, Riot states that “Accounts involved in MMR manipulation and manipulative behavior result in immediate suspension of the accounts, removal of Honor level and exclusion from the ranked rewards of the season/Split” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024k)</2>.<3>p. 462</3>

When setting out to explain MMR, Riot expressly states: “Your MMR is… a secret!” and justifies that “it was specially created to work with back-end systems” aimed at placing “each person in a balanced match”, which is why it cannot be dissociated from these systems without loss of context.<1>p. 94</1>

The legal point this example illuminates is that accumulated symbolic capital is held under a regime of disciplined permanence, since the platform not only describes standards of conduct but reserves to itself a power of intervention capable of downgrading enjoyment through functional limitations, interaction restrictions, redefinitions of progress and, in extreme cases, the very extinction of participation, with measures that can be triggered even when the specific conduct has not been listed in advance as inappropriate <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>. The risk of sanction thus falls not only on formal access but on the integrity of agency and on the maintenance of symbolic identity as a public position, since the system of rewards and eligibility turns prestige into something at once desirable and vulnerable to private governance.<3>p. 462</3>

Read with care, the case does not say that disciplining conduct is illegitimate. The question is not the abstract legitimacy of that discipline but the consequence of its falling on signs and positions that make up the value enjoyed as symbolic identity. The case shows the lawyer what form the relevant loss may take, whether loss of position, persistent disqualification, erasure of signs of distinction or restrictions that make participation in internal circuits of value unfeasible. It also offers a path of proof that does not depend on the player's own account, because requirements, tables and announcements are the company's own documents and show how the system assigns social value to the object.

The question at issue is not the abstract legitimacy of this discipline, but the structural consequence of its falling on signs and positions that make up the value enjoyed as symbolic identity.<1>p. 462</1>

In practical terms, what the environment recognizes as merit becomes, at the same time, an instrument of capture through disciplinary asymmetry, since preserving the possibility of receiving and sustaining signs of prestige comes to require continuous self-adjustment in the face of administratively controlled criteria and determinations <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024k)</2>. In this frame, the relevant downgrade may consist of loss of position, persistent disqualification, erasure of signs of distinction, systematic instability of recognition or restrictions that make participation in internal circuits of value unfeasible.<3>p. 462-463</3>

The minimum sign of proof lies not in a subjective account of sadness or frustration, but in the objective demonstration of how the system itself assigns social value to the object, through internal markers, visibility, participation requirements, access restrictions and reputational effects.<1>p. 673</1>
What consequences does the recognition of these goods produce?

The first concerns how the contract is read. Clause 2.3 of Riot's Terms of Service, examined as a case in the chapter on remedies, provides that the user loses access to the account, the data, the in-game currency and the virtual content when the account is terminated. The same text adds that termination does not limit or affect rights the user may have under data protection or consumer protection laws. Clause 4.5 of the same Terms reserves to the company the right to delete, alter, remove, reprice or transfer any game content, with or without notice, to the extent permitted by law, and promises a refund or replacement when the company completely withdraws recently purchased virtual products. Read in full, the clauses show the power of erasure that the first one expresses, and they also show a contract that subjects that power to the law and provides for reparation in one narrow case, the complete withdrawal of a recent purchase.

The clause is valuable because it lays bare the problem: what is lost is not merely an isolated item, but the overall position of enjoyment, the history, the inventory, the trajectory and the practical continuity of one's place in the ecosystem. Here exclusivity is exercised as a power of complete erasure of the consumed experience, which prevents treating sanction, exclusion or rollback as mere internal adjustments without existential legal relevance.<1>p. 540-541</1>

If your account is terminated you will no longer have access to your account, including the associated data or the Virtual Content (including the Game Currency) (although this does not limit or affect any rights you may have under data protection or consumer protection laws).<1>p. 540</1>

In an effort to constantly improve the Riot Services, develop our games and keep the Riot Services safe, fun and secure, we have the right to delete, alter, move, remove, repackage, reprice or transfer any and all Game Content, including Virtual Content, in whole or in part, at any time, with or without prior notice to you, to the extent permitted by law.<1>p. 613</1>
If we decide to completely withdraw certain Virtual Products that you have recently purchased, we will provide you with a refund or a replacement.<1>p. 614</1>

The second concerns the framing. When the governance program not only downgrades enjoyment but also produces relevant risk or actual harm to goods of a personal dimension, the case may come close to a defect in the service. One example is a combination of opaque sanctions, severe reputational exclusions, erasures of history, a permanent threat of loss and the practical impossibility of contesting any of it. The distinction follows the CDC, which separates the protection of safety from the protection of adequacy, and the chapter on the unlawful act of architecture deals with this transition.

There are, however, cases in which abusive teleology goes beyond functional inadequacy and comes close to a defect in the service. This occurs when the governance program not only downgrades enjoyment but produces relevant risk or actual harm to legal goods of a personal dimension, especially when the combination of opaque sanctions, severe reputational exclusions, erasures of history, permanent threat of loss and practical impossibility of contestation reaches personal integrity, biographical continuity or symbolic identity. The distinction matters because the CDC, in its own architecture, already separates the protection of safety from the protection of adequacy.<1>p. 675-676</1>

The third concerns governance. Whoever administers access, permanence, visibility, sanctions and participation tracks also administers inclusion and exclusion in the digital social space, and this is the source of the parameters of private due process that the chapter on remedies develops. The LGPD adds further support. The use of data linked to the trajectory must be compatible with the purposes disclosed to the data subject, under Article 6, item II, of the LGPD, intelligible to the data subject, under Article 6, item VI, of the LGPD, and backed by the secure management of records and trails, in light of Article 46 of the LGPD.

The institutional consequence of this reading falls on the platform's governance itself. If it administers access, permanence, visibility, sanctions and participation tracks, then it also administers inclusion and exclusion in the digital social space. From this follows the need for minimum parameters of private due process: verifiable reasoning, decisional coherence, procedural predictability and intelligible avenues of contestation.<1>p. 541</1>

The use of data linked to the consumer's trajectory, history and digital biography must remain compatible with the purposes disclosed and with the context of the relationship, must be intelligible to the data subject, and does not eliminate the rights to confirm the existence of, access, correct, delete or port the data processed. It also presupposes secure management of relevant records and trails.<1>p. 542</1>

“Art. 6 Personal data processing activities shall observe good faith and the following principles: [...] II - adequacy: compatibility of the processing with the purposes disclosed to the data subject, in accordance with the context of the processing;” <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2026]a)</2>.<3>p. 542</3>

“Art. 46. Processing agents must adopt security, technical and administrative measures capable of protecting personal data from unauthorized access [...].” <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2026]a)</2>.<3>p. 542</3>
Isn't protecting a trajectory just protecting hurt feelings?

The first objection is sentimentalism, the claim that protecting trajectory and reputation would mean protecting hurt feelings. But the injury is measured by the attribute objectively affected, and symbolic identity is a public, collectively verifiable position. The second is that history and records would be a data matter, foreign to consumption, but the administration of these elements is part of the very regime of enjoyment and interferes with the consumer's informational and biographical integrity. The third is the lack of full ownership. Article 24, item VII, of the Copyright Law answers it, because it shows that the legal order already accepts minimum duties of access to preserve the memory of an immaterial object under a third party's control, without making the consumer an author.

The digital experience can reach legally relevant dimensions of personal integrity precisely because data protection, informational self-determination and the free development of personality make up the existential core of the person in an informational environment <1>Laprano</1><2>(Canavez; Andrade; Laprano, 2021, p. 139; p. 148; p. 155-156)</2>. That is why the administration of these elements cannot be treated as a simple “data topic” set apart from the consumer relationship. It is part of the very regime of enjoyment and directly interferes with the consumer's informational and biographical integrity.<3>p. 535</3>

The Copyright Law recognizes, in Article 24, item VII, the author's moral right to access a single and rare copy of the work that is legitimately in the possession of another in order to preserve its memory. The point is not to turn the consumer into an author, nor to transplant the regime of authors' moral rights into the consumer field. The point is narrower and more elegant: the Brazilian legal order already accepts, in another domain, that preserving memory linked to an immaterial object under a third party's control may justify minimum positive duties to provide access and enable recording. This suffices to dispose of the superficial objection that the absence of full ownership would by itself eliminate any legal relevance of interests in memory, preservation and continuity.<1>p. 542</1>

The fourth is that of constitutional inflation, which would turn the platform into a State. Digital citizenship, however, is a strict, functional description of how certain private ecosystems concentrate conditions of participation, recognition and reputation, and the platform operates as a private environment of public relevance insofar as it structures opportunities for expression, participation and recognition. The fifth is that opacity would make these losses undecidable. The answer follows Ferraz Jr. Legal technique does not suspend its action in the face of opacity, because it organizes criteria that make opacity bearable, and the act of deciding converts undecidable incompatibilities into decidable alternatives, without promising harmony.

The reference to digital citizenship does not operate as a constitutionalizing displacement nor as an inflated metaphor, but as a functional description of the way certain private ecosystems came to concentrate relevant conditions of social participation, recognition and circulation of reputation.<1>p. 464-465</1>

The argument is represented strictly. The platform operates as a private environment of public relevance to the extent that it structures practical opportunities for expression, participation and recognition, and continuous consumption places the consumer in a position of functional dependence on these conditions.<1>p. 465</1>

Under the methodological constraints already consolidated, legal technique does not suspend its action in the face of opacity, since it organizes criteria to make it bearable under normative binding and institutional pressure for decision, expanding uncertainties in an action-oriented way <1>Jr.</1><2>(Ferraz Jr., 2003, [p. 87])</2>.<3>p. 468</3>

Seen this way, the absorption of insecurity justifies turning initially diffuse losses into controllable segments, since the act of deciding converts undecidable incompatibilities into decidable alternatives, even if it later generates new incompatibilities, sometimes more complex than the earlier ones, without this transformation being mistaken for a promise of harmony <1>Jr.</1><2>(Ferraz Jr., 2003, [p. 312-313])</2>.<3>p. 468</3>
Does any discomfort become an injury?

Delimiting the categories keeps personal integrity, symbolic identity, symbolic captivity, identity captivity and digital citizenship from becoming expansive labels that absorb any discomfort from the ordinary frictions of the market. The aim is not to raise the consumer's experience to a psychological yardstick, nor to turn trivial frustrations, aesthetic preferences or normal service fluctuations into matters of reinforced protection. Nor is it to attribute unlawfulness to technology as such or to replace dogmatic criteria with moral disapproval of the business model. The matrix of losses, moreover, is not meant to exhaust the phenomenon but to make it decidable by criteria.

Thus the protection of integrity and identity, when they operate as functional dimensions of enjoyment in private environments of public relevance, can be formulated as a protective core without abstract moralism, provided it remains tied to criteria of relevance and to standards of verifiability capable of converting this core into decidable losses in the IOC regime. This incorporation requires, however, explicit delimitation to keep personal integrity, symbolic identity, symbolic captivity, identity captivity and digital citizenship from becoming expansive labels capable of absorbing any discomfort arising from ordinary market frictions.<1>p. 467</1>

This is not about raising the consumer's experience to a psychological parameter nor about turning trivial frustrations, aesthetic preferences or normal service fluctuations into matters of reinforced protection. Nor is it about attributing unlawfulness to technology as such or replacing dogmatic criteria with moral disapproval of the business model.<1>p. 467</1>

The matrix of losses relating to personal integrity and symbolic identity, as outlined here, is not meant to exhaust the phenomenon but to make it decidable by criteria, opening the way to standards of verifiability and restoration compatible with continued enjoyment.<1>p. 468</1>

On the side of personality, the limits are equally express. The consumer's integrity may comprise the preservation of minimum conditions of biographical continuity, built trajectory, symbolic insertion and stability of enjoyment, without dissolving the analysis into psychologism or displacing the CDC from the center of protection. The reinforcements from the LGPD do not make the consumer the absolute owner of everything the platform records, the copyright parallel does not turn the consumer into an author, restoration of the position of enjoyment applies where appropriate, and moral damages are reserved for qualified and objectifiable hypotheses, without reaching mere annoyance.

The consumer's integrity, in continuous digital ecosystems, may comprise the preservation of minimum conditions of biographical continuity, built trajectory, symbolic insertion and stability of enjoyment, without this implying dissolving the analysis into psychologism or removing from the CDC its protective centrality.<1>p. 536-537</1>

These provisions do not turn the consumer into the absolute owner of everything the platform records, but they reinforce that the consumer's digital biography is not raw mass entirely unavailable to the data subject and that the administration of the memory of enjoyment needs to remain controllable, intelligible and minimally accessible.<1>p. 542</1>

The consequence is not to make the consumer an author, but to recognize that erasures, resets, inventory exclusions, suppressions of history and sanctions that eliminate the biography built in the environment require verifiable reasoning, minimum preservation of records and, where appropriate, restoration through reinstatement of the position of enjoyment.<1>p. 543</1>

Nor is the civil law taxonomy that divides digital goods into patrimonial, existential and mixed the point of entry. It remains useful for ownership, succession and circulation, but once the IOC is qualified, the pertinent question becomes the regime of enjoyment that the asset sustains. The protected goods are therefore not shown by classifying the skin, the account or the title as an existential good, but by the position of enjoyment that governance has downgraded.

When this qualification asserts itself, the pertinent initial question ceases to be about the patrimonial or existential nature of the asset and becomes about the regime of enjoyment that this asset sustains within the environment that produces it.<1>p. 571</1>

The patrimonial, existential and mixed taxonomy, considered in itself, is neither discarded nor demonized. It remains a useful instrument when the conflict genuinely turns on ownership, succession, post mortem destination or inter vivos disposition of the digital asset, cases in which the civil law floor offers a technically adequate answer.<1>p. 571</1>

How to read this doctrine

Continuous digital consumption confronts the jurist with a conflict that the grammar of defect and accident captures poorly, because the loss usually arrives as technical normality rather than as an event. From this follow the problem and the hypothesis that organize the chapters ahead, the normative scope in which they operate, the choice of a game as a laboratory and the weight of each kind of proof.
What conflict does the jurist need to learn to see?

In one kind of consumption the consumer thinks they are standing on their own ground, but they only move on ground that is granted, revocable and reconfigurable. What they acquired depends on a continuous administration that presents itself as technical normality, and its value lies in what it allows them to do, what it signals and the place it holds in the ecosystem. When everything changes and the consumer no longer feels the same, this is neither subjective drama nor mere annoyance but the foreseeable consequence of a regime in which use value, symbolic value and continuity of enjoyment are subject to the governance of third parties.
There is a type of consumption in which the subject thinks they are walking on their own ground, but only moves within a granted, revocable and fully reconfigurable floor.<1>p. 21</1>

Access, permanence and even the meaning of what was acquired depend on a continuous administration that presents itself not as management, but as technical normality. The object's value does not lie only in what it is. It lies in what it allows one to do, in what it signals, in the place it occupies in the ecosystem and in the way this ecosystem recognizes or erases its bearer.<1>p. 21</1>

The CDC was tailored for a world in which risk shows its face and harm leaves traces. In continuous platform-governed consumption, enjoyment depends on changeable rules, invisible curation, sanctions and updates, and the injury ceases to be the failure that escaped control and becomes the one that was converted into a business model. The traditional categories end up treating as after-sales what, in practice, is the core of the object.
The “product” is not a stable thing, it is an administered position.<1>p. 32</1>
The Brazilian Consumer Protection Code was tailored for a world in which risk shows its face and harm leaves direct traces on the body, the mind and property.<1>p. 32</1>
Enjoyment depends on changeable rules, on invisible curation, on sanctions, on updates and on an authority that does not present itself as such.<1>p. 32</1>
Causality itself changes, because the injury is no longer the failure that escaped control, but the one that was converted into a “legitimate” business model.<1>p. 32</1>

The consequence is a growing mismatch between the way consumption is actually organized, in highly complex and continuously reconfigured digital environments, and the traditional categories mobilized for its protection, which end up treating as “after-sales” what, in practice, is the very core of the object.<1>p. 31-32</1>

The injury rarely announces itself as an explicit scam and usually comes as administered normality, a promise of experience, an incentive to stay and a cost one learns to call inevitable. That is why the decisive conflict is not only what happened, but how what happened can be said without being downgraded to noise, in a dispute filtered by recording formats, evidentiary criteria and limits on access to information. Consumer protection can only act when what appears as the functioning of the system is seen again as a controllable decision and, therefore, as responsibility.

Why is the problem dogmatic, and not only technological?

The obstacle lies in how the Code is read, not in any lack of a normative basis. A strictly material ontology reduces the product to the delivery of a physical medium or of a performance that can be completed, when Article 3, paragraph 1, of the Brazilian Consumer Protection Code (CDC)<1><2>1</2></1> already contains the opening needed for goods without a stable corporeal medium. Put as an image, the IOC subdivides a plot that the 1990 legislator had already marked out and that doctrine left vacant. The gap has a cost, because every stable dogmatic gap tends to become a business model, risk that an improbable sanction fails to restrain gets priced in, and dogmatics, by omission, may end up becoming part of the arrangement that shifts losses onto the consumer.
The guiding hypothesis, confirmed in the end, was that the difficulty did not lie in an absence of normative basis, but in the persistence of an ontologically impoverished reading<1>p. 793</1>

It must be recognized, however, that this expansibility of Brazilian Consumer Law has been held back by a strictly material ontology, which insists on reducing the product to the delivery of a physical medium or of a discrete and finalizable performance. Article 3, paragraph 1, of the Consumer Protection Code already contains the normative opening necessary for the recognition of goods that circulate without a stable corporeal medium and whose enjoyment depends on continuous technical and organizational conditions. The Immaterial Object of Consumption (IOC) presents itself, in this sense, as the definitive subdivision of a plot that the 1990 legislator had already marked out, although contemporary doctrine has kept it in the condition of a vacant lot.<1>p. 24-25</1>
Keeping this lot vacant is not merely a theoretical problem. It produces foreseeable institutional effects, because every stable dogmatic gap tends to be converted into a business model.<1>p. 25</1>

When oversight is rare and sanction is improbable, risk ceases to act as a brake and comes to be priced, as if it were merely an operating cost. Dogmatics, by omission, may end up becoming part of the very arrangement that naturalizes the transfer of losses to the consumer.<1>p. 25</1>

The dispute between the United States and China at the WTO serves as a methodological analogy. When the unlawful act is designed through thresholds and metrics, the boundary between lawful and unlawful becomes an optimization parameter, with profit through scale and repetition below the punishable threshold, and on platforms the transfer of losses may operate through microdecisions that each user perceives as noise. Hence the focus on categories capable of seeing patterns.

When the institutional design of the unlawful act operates through thresholds and metrics, the boundary between lawful and unlawful ceases to function as an effective prohibition and comes to operate as an optimization parameter of the business model itself, in which profit is realized not through a high margin on few units, but through scale and repetition below the punishable threshold.<1>p. 26</1>

In platform-governed digital ecosystems, the extraction and transfer of losses can also operate through scattered microdecisions, unilateral reconfigurations, frictions and informational asymmetries, which are perceived as noise by the individual user, but become economically significant at scale. The reference thus functions as an origin by analogy and also as a justification of the epistemological focus on legal categories capable of seeing patterns, making technical decisions visible and enabling qualification, proof and imputation in regimes of private governance.<1>p. 26</1>

The move to the constitutional level follows from the constitutionalization of law. As Freitas and Clemente recall, fundamental rights radiate effects onto private relationships, above all when those relationships concentrate powers capable of degrading relevant existential positions. When the platform alone organizes access, permanence, visibility, proof and sanction, what is at work is no longer simple freedom of contract in a neutral environment but a private exercise of power capable of affecting fundamental rights.

If fundamental rights are no longer understood only as barriers raised against the State and now radiate effects onto the various branches of the legal order, then the private relationship can no longer be treated as a space immune to the incidence of constitutional values, above all when it concentrates powers capable of conditioning, restricting or degrading relevant existential positions of the subjects involved <1>Clemente</1><2>(Freitas; Clemente, 2011, p. 160-161)</2>.<3>p. 23</3>

In other words, when the platform unilaterally organizes access, permanence, visibility, proof and sanction, what is at stake is no longer simple freedom of contract in a neutral environment, but a private exercise of power concretely capable of affecting the consumer's fundamental rights.<1>p. 24</1>

Dante's Inferno, stripped of its sacred language, also serves as a heuristic instrument to separate the unlawful act that manifests as force in an event from the one that stabilizes as fraud of design and governance. The last circle is made of ice, and the betrayal it holds is cold and discreet, hard to grasp through common intuition. Without abandoning the CDC's accidents and defects, the protection of dignity calls for a category capable of seeing the unlawful act before the event, when design makes the cry for help inaudible.

It is not a harm that screams, but a structure that silences, that sickens the bond by stiffening it, that makes the loss naturalized, and that induces the subject themself to passively occupy the position in which they are harmed.<1>p. 35</1>

This is neither sacred language nor theological judgment, but a heuristic instrument to distinguish, on the legal level, differences of structure between unlawful acts that manifest as force in an event and unlawful acts that stabilize as fraud of design and governance.<1>p. 33</1>
The last circle also adds a detail decisive for this reading: it is not an environment marked by fire, but ice.<1>p. 35</1>
Betrayal, ultimately, is cold, discreet, motionless, and precisely for this reason substantially harder to understand from common intuition.<1>p. 35</1>

Therefore, the traditional accidents and defects described under the Brazilian consumer codification are not being abandoned; rather, support is being offered for the view that, when technique is carried to its ultimate consequences, the protection of dignity requires a category capable of seeing evil before the scream, the unlawful act before the event, which manifests itself under a design capable of making any cry for help inaudible. The platform disqualifies the consumer as a subject who deserves to be heard, turning the search for justice into mere noise that it can administer itself.<1>p. 35-36</1>
What is the central problem, and what is the hypothesis?

The central problem is how to reconstruct the consumer protection regime in the face of digital goods and interactive entertainment platforms without breaking with the CDC and the Constitution, making it responsive to the technical and media order. More specifically, the question is how Consumer Law can face the risks of continued exposure to digital objects that mobilize attention, affectivity, identity and assets under business models oriented to the maximum extraction of value.

It is in this context that the central problem is situated: how to reconstruct the consumer protection regime in light of the reality of digital goods and interactive entertainment platforms, without breaking with the normative framework of the Consumer Protection Code and the Constitution? And, at the same time, how to make it responsive to the new technical-media order? More specifically: in what way can Brazilian Consumer Law recognize and face the risks derived from the continued exposure of individuals to digital objects that intensely mobilize their attention, their affectivity, their identity, and even their assets under the logic of business models oriented to the maximum extraction of value?<1>p. 33</1>

The hypothesis is that this update depends on a legal-analytical category capable of capturing what is specific about digital goods in a platform environment. That category is the Immaterial Object of Consumption, an infrastructure concept that gives concrete form to the immaterial product of Article 3, paragraph 1, of the CDC<1><2>1</2></1> and shifts the focus from the conformity of the corporeal object to the governance of the functional and symbolic architectures of the experience. The factual vulnerability of Article 4, item I, of the CDC<3><4>2</4></3> takes on a form of its own there, linked to mediation by signs and interfaces and intensified by hypercuratorial anticipation, which projects images of performance, reward and future experience without offering, in the same measure, real conditions for verifying them. Abusive teleology makes it possible to qualify, under strict criteria, the situations in which the architecture is designed to exploit this vulnerability systematically, and protection must also safeguard the functional integrity of goods and the user's personal and symbolic identity.

The hypothesis guiding the work is that this update depends on the formulation of a legal-analytical category capable of capturing the specificity of digital goods in a platform environment. To this end, the thesis proposes the Immaterial Object of Consumption (IOC) as an infrastructure concept that gives concrete form, on the dogmatic level, to the notion of “immaterial product” already enacted in the Brazilian legal order under Article 3, paragraph 1, of the CDC<1><2>1</2></1>, shifting the focus from the mere conformity of a corporeal object to the governance of functional and symbolic architectures that structure the consumer's experience.<3>p. 34</3>

From this perspective, it is argued that the consumer's factual vulnerability, expressly recognized in Article 4, item I, of the CDC<1><2>2</2></1>, takes on a form of its own in digital environments, linked to mediation by signs, interfaces and private criteria of visibility and enjoyment. This vulnerability is intensified by practices of hypercuratorial anticipation, through which the platform projects images of performance, reward and future experience without offering, in the same measure, real conditions of verification and control by the consumer.<3>p. 34</3>

In this framework, the operational concept of abusive teleology makes it possible to qualify, under strict criteria, situations in which the architecture of the environment is designed to systematically exploit the consumer's semiotic vulnerability, instrumentalizing their attention and their symbolic identity in favor of revenue maximization. Consumer protection, then, needs to be reconstructed so as to protect not only physical or economic integrity, but equally the functional integrity of the goods acquired and the user's personal and symbolic identity, both continuously projected onto the Immaterial Objects of Consumption, which are responsible for structuring life in the digital ecosystem.<1>p. 34</1>

The first is descriptive and recognizes the law of the platform, a technically executable private ordering that functions as the effective floor of conduct before enacted law manages to name it, and which has its own chapter ahead. The requirement is consistent with Miguel Reale, for whom Law only reaches reality when it converts facts and values into criteria, and with Tércio Sampaio Ferraz Jr., for whom, without categories of structure and recurrence, the decision fragments into microevents.

What one seeks to qualify is the case in which the exploitative purpose is inscribed in the very architecture of the service and reproduces itself as a regularity, through choices of design, curation and sanction that make enjoyment dependent on asymmetries the consumer can neither decode nor audit. Why isn't the answer a new law?

The answer lies neither in a new law nor in a microsystem for games or platforms. The Immaterial Object of Consumption is an interpretive update already internal to the CDC and derived from the constitutional principles that inform it, and the reconstruction works on the law in force, without normative invention. Behind it lies a reading of Consumer Law as a deliberately expandable technical idiom, made to recognize shifting asymmetries and to capture abuses that do not announce themselves as deviations.

The IOC is not a new microsystem, but a new key of interpretation, a way of reading the CDC itself and the Constitution, leading them to the centrality of flows of code, images, sounds and narratives in the configuration of digital consumer relationships.<1>p. 34</1>

Instead of proposing an autonomous regulatory microsystem for “electronic games” or “digital platforms”, what is being proposed is a demonstration that the Immaterial Object of Consumption is a form of interpretive update that, in dogmatic terms, is already internal to the CDC itself and derived from the constitutional principles that inform it, with special attention to the guarantee of recognition of the consumer's vulnerability and to the social function of intellectual property.<1>p. 36</1>

The dogmatic reconstruction operates on the law in force and seeks to produce a justifiable interpretation in light of recognizable normative parameters, without normative invention and without a proposal for an autonomous microsystem.<1>p. 48</1>

In this scenario, Consumer Law presents itself as a deliberately expandable technical idiom, built to recognize changing asymmetries and to capture abuses that do not announce themselves as deviations, preserving the promise of protection even when the market sheds its skin.<1>p. 23</1>

The method is the coordination of sources. The Constitution, the CDC and intellectual property are not read as watertight blocks but through a coordinated reading of the sources that bear on the same relationship, with the dialogue of sources serving as a discipline of interpretation rather than as a topic in its own right. Article 7 of the CDC<1><2>3</2></1> provides support, since it states that the rights in the Code do not exclude others arising from domestic legislation, treaties, regulations and general principles. The ambition is to rearticulate the categories without letting exclusivity, licensing and technical powers act as a title of immunity against review for adequacy, transparency and abusiveness.

On the legal-normative level, the proposed reconstruction does not operate through a compartmentalized reading of the sources, as if the Constitution, the Consumer Protection Code and the intellectual property regimes applied in watertight and mutually exclusive blocks.<1>p. 48</1>

As a methodological criterion of normative articulation, the path adopts a coordinated reading of sources that bear simultaneously on the same governed consumer relationship, especially when the conflict involves, at the same time, constitutional protection of the person and of the consumer, consumer-law rules on supply and the structures of exclusivity, licensing and technical control proper to intellectual property rights. Seen this way, the theory of the dialogue of sources appears less as an autonomous topic than as a methodological discipline of interpretation, allowing a systematically controlled reconstruction of the problem without artificially isolating the relevant legal regimes.<1>p. 48</1>

Here Article 7 of the CDC<1><2>3</2></1> provides a relevant normative point of support, by making explicit that the rights provided for in the Code do not exclude others arising from domestic legislation, treaties, regulations and general principles, reinforcing the openness of the consumer microsystem to coordination with other applicable normative sources.<3>p. 48-49</3>

The dogmatic ambition is to interpret and rearticulate categories of the Consumer Protection Code and of intellectual property rights under the regime of the Immaterial Object of Consumption, preserving the protective matrix and refusing to let exclusivity, licensing or technical powers operate as a title of immunity against review for adequacy, transparency and abusiveness.<1>p. 49</1>
Within what normative scope does this doctrine operate?

The scope is centered on the constitutional order of consumer protection and of the economic order, which limits the exploitation of asymmetries, structural opacity and private power, and on the CDC as the matrix of protection. Intellectual property enters with a functional status, as the grammar of access control and licensing, and licenses and technical restrictions are read as legal-technological infrastructure, without authorizing the degradation of promises of adequacy and restoration.

The normative basis brought to bear is the constitutional order of consumer protection and of the economic order, which limits the exploitation of asymmetries, structural opacity and forms of private power capable of reorganizing access, information and risk.<1>p. 54</1>

On this axis, the Consumer Protection Code is preserved as the central matrix of protection, while intellectual property legislation is brought in with a functional status, as the legal grammar of access control and licensing that, in digital markets, structures the very way utilities circulate and are enjoyed.<1>p. 54</1>

Licenses and technical restrictions are treated not merely as contractual content but as legal-technological infrastructure that delimits what may be used, for how long, on what conditions and under which unilateral powers of modulation, without this operating as a blanket authorization to degrade promises of adequacy, comparability and restoration in consumption.<1>p. 54</1>

In software, temporality is an express legal category. Articles 7 and 8 of Law 9,609/1998<1><2>4</2></1> require the license agreement, the tax document and the media or packaging to state the period of technical validity of the version, and they oblige whoever markets the program to provide complementary technical services during that period, even if the program is withdrawn from circulation, without prejudice to compensation for losses. Updates, end of support and maintenance are therefore not neutral events beyond the protection of adequacy and transparency. Technical validity does not require every change to be announced in advance. It works as a checkpoint between operational variation and relevant reconfiguration, without making the evolution of the service unlawful.

Article 7 requires the license agreement, the tax document and the media and packaging to state, in easily legible form, the period of technical validity of the version marketed, and Article 8 turns this period into an obligation to provide complementary technical services for the proper functioning of the program during its technical validity, including when it is withdrawn from commercial circulation, without prejudice to compensation for losses.<1>p. 51</1>

Articles 7 and 8 of Law 9,609/1998<1><2>4</2></1> link a duty to inform about technical validity with a duty of complementary technical support for proper functioning during that period, including after withdrawal from circulation, which rules out treating “updates”, “end of support” and “maintenance” as neutral events beyond the reach of the protection of adequacy and transparency.<3>p. 55</3>

In services built on continuous updating, the reference to technical validity does not operate as a requirement to announce specific changes or a schedule of modulations in advance, which is plainly impossible in factual and operational terms. It works as a checkpoint for qualifying duties of information, support and restoration when the exercise of unilateral power significantly reconfigures the content of what is supplied and shifts onto the consumer losses arising from this mutability, without turning the evolving dynamics of the service into unlawfulness in itself.<1>p. 51-52</1>

From this follows a consequence that runs through every chapter. Governance is treated as the continuous performance of the relationship, so that sanctions, blocks, account restrictions, degradations and recalibrations of access function as performance, nonperformance and functional coercion. A relevant loss no longer depends on material subtraction, and persistent changes in access, position and conditions of use may reshape the link between promise and delivery, provided they can be identified by controllable criteria.

The conflict no longer revolves around a one-off delivery and is reconstructed as a dispute over continuity, functional stability and the actual content of the performance in objects administered over time, under private powers exercised at the contractual, technical and organizational levels.<1>p. 55</1>

In doctrinal terms, the scope recognizes that platform governance operates as the continuous performance of the relationship, insofar as internal sanctions, blocks, account restrictions, degradations and recalibrations of access function as forms of performance, nonperformance and functional coercion built into the very experience of use.<1>p. 55</1>

The Consumer Protection Code remains the central matrix of protection, while the intellectual property regime comes in with a functional status, describing contemporary forms of enclosure and circulation of utilities through licenses, technical conditions and powers of modulation. This coordination makes it possible to reconstruct verifiable criteria for qualifying object, legitimate expectation manufactured as a promise, enjoyment, loss and restoration in platform-governed ecosystems, without turning exclusivity into a claim of immunity from the CDC. It also prevents the legal relevance of losses from being made conditional on material subtraction, accepting that persistent changes in access, position and internal conditions of use may reshape the link between promise, legitimate expectation and delivery in a legally relevant way, provided they can be identified by controllable criteria.<1>p. 52</1>

Criminal liability, broadcasting, software taxation and personal data protection as autonomous axes fall outside the direct scope.

At the sector level, interactive entertainment is adopted as a privileged field of observation because it concentrates mechanisms of retention, artificial scarcity, reputation, continuous administration of identity and positional modulation, making visible the frictions that continuous digital services create for traditional categories of adequacy and restoration.<1>p. 55</1>

In this context, the Legal Framework for Electronic Games is treated as an institutional reference for a minimum framing of the sector, useful for situating categories, concerns and regulatory language tied to the economic and cultural recognition of the activity, without turning the inquiry into a legislative inventory and without shifting the decisional core to the current state of the legislative effort to regulate it.<1>p. 55</1>

Why can a game serve as a laboratory?

Because it is treated as play, interactive entertainment shows with less varnish the structures that other sectors present as convenience or innovation. Reward cycles, retention metrics, visibility management and friction engineering are openly acknowledged there, while platforms regarded as serious present them as neutrality, personalization or efficiency. Games therefore offer a laboratory for what recurs in communication, work, learning and consumption in general, where the same effects tend to pass for inevitable.
Studying games, in this sense, is not choosing a minor object. It is choosing the place where the mechanisms show most clearly.<1>p. 22</1>

Because it is treated as play, interactive entertainment ends up exposing, with less modesty and less varnish, structures that in other sectors appear disguised as convenience, innovation or the mere organization of a service. In games, reward cycles, retention metrics, visibility management, friction engineering and behavior management are acknowledged more openly. On platforms commonly taken seriously, the same set of techniques appears under the guise of neutrality, personalization or efficiency.<1>p. 22</1>

If the experience of interactive entertainment allows one to see, almost with the naked eye, the production of dependence, the manufacture of symbolic value, the conversion of routine into attachment and the naturalization of asymmetries, then it offers a privileged laboratory for understanding what recurs in ecosystems of communication, work, learning, reputation and consumption in general. The difference is that, outside the game, the same effects tend to be presented as inevitable, and not as architectural choices.<1>p. 23</1>

Why is the Riot Games ecosystem the laboratory?

The laboratory was chosen for its analytical usefulness, not out of thematic preference. The ecosystem is a continuous digital service, in which the product is a prolonged, calibrated and revisable relationship. Its intangible objects and performances depend entirely on a private technical and normative apparatus to exist and produce value. Governance is dense, with rules of conduct, metrics, incentives, sanctions and periodic reorganization of the environment. And mutability is visible, since substantial changes can occur without a new contract and often without the average user understanding them, while public traces make it possible to triangulate text, communication and enforcement.

This ecosystem was selected not out of thematic preference but on criteria of analytical usefulness. First, it is a continuous digital service, whose experience is mediated by rules and updates, so that the “product” is not a one-off delivery but a prolonged, calibrated and revisable relationship.<1>p. 56</1>

Second, the economic dynamics sustaining it are organized around digital objects and intangible performances that, although perceived as consumer goods, depend entirely on a private technical and normative apparatus to exist, circulate and produce functional value. Third, governance is highly dense, since the platform not only offers and monetizes but also disciplines conduct, sets internal metrics, redistributes incentives, applies sanctions and periodically reorganizes the very environment in which the promised experience takes place and, in doing so, consolidates the consumer's legitimate expectation.<1>p. 56</1>

Moreover, the ecosystem makes the structural mutability of digital consumption especially visible, since substantial changes can occur without any change of ownership, without a new explicit contract and often without the average user properly grasping the practical reach of the change.<1>p. 57</1>

Finally, it is an environment with enough public traces and documentable material to allow referenced anchoring, with minimal triangulation between normative texts, institutional communication and enforcement practices, reducing the risk that the analysis rests on subjective impression or personal experience.<1>p. 57</1>

The choice fell on the Riot Games ecosystem, centered on League of Legends, because of the density and diversity of the public traces it produces.
